explicit_validation.explanation: The paper explicitly validates their LLM-as-a-judge evaluator against human annotations on a subset of 120 episodes, calculating accuracy of the LLM evaluator against majority vote labels and reporting inter-annotator agreement metrics

prompts.notes: The full prompt is available in Appendix J, contains definitions and examples of truthfulness behaviors, and follows a structured format requiring rationale

guidelines.notes: Detailed guidelines with definitions and examples of truthful behaviors provided in Appendix C, annotators had omniscient access to episode context

sample_size.notes: Validation conducted on randomly sampled subset (120 episodes) from all generated interactions

quantitative_scores.notes: Overall accuracy against human majority vote

validation_results.summary_finding: The LLM evaluator achieves 85% accuracy against human majority vote, indicating it can be reliably used for quantitative truthfulness assessment with strong agreement across most scenarios.

human_only_criteria: fine-grained distinction between concealment and equivocation
criteria_mapping.notes: Human evaluation used fine-grained classification while LLM used coarse-grained; validation was performed using coarse-grained categories where partial lie combined concealment and equivocation
